species.name: Marandu grass
species.description: This African grass is widely planted as cattle forage in Brazil. It forms dense tussocks in pastures and disturbed ground.
species.use: People plant it as cattle forage.
species.fireNote: Dry standing blades can add fine surface fuel.

species.plainUse: People grow it as food for cattle.

species.name: Guinea grass
species.description: This African grass is planted for pasture in tropical regions. It can spread into open disturbed areas and form tall clumps.
species.use: People plant it for cattle forage.
species.fireNote: Dry grass litter can carry surface fire.

species.plainUse: People grow it as food for cattle.

species.name: Signal grass
species.taxonomyNote: Some taxonomic backbones accept Brachiaria decumbens as the name and treat Urochloa decumbens as a synonym.
species.description: This African grass was introduced for pasture and erosion control. A study in the Carajás National Forest in Pará found lower natural regeneration where it was present.
species.use: People plant it for pasture and erosion control.
species.fireNote: Dry grass litter can carry surface fire.

species.plainUse: People plant it for cattle and to hold soil in place.

species.name: Trumpet tree
species.description: This Guianas to northern Brazil tree often grows in secondary forest and road edges. Its large lobed leaves and hollow-looking trunk make it useful for field identification.
species.use: Traditional medicine records describe leaf and bark preparations in French Guiana. Uses vary by community.
species.fireNote: Leaf litter can add surface material after drying.

sources.title: Medicinal Plants of the Guianas: Cecropia obtusa
Plants of the World Online: Cecropia obtusa

species.plainUse: Some communities in French Guiana use its leaves and bark in traditional medicine.

species.name: South American traveller's palm
species.description: This native Guianas and Amazon plant has a tall pseudostem and very large fan-like leaves. It is an herb rather than a true palm tree.
species.use: In Suriname, guides record leaves folded and woven for roof mats.
species.fireNote: Old leaves can add material to the forest floor after drying.

sources.title: WFO Monographs: Phenakospermum guyannense
Guide to the vascular plants of central French Guiana

species.plainUse: In Suriname people weave its leaves into roof mats.

species.name: Bacaba palm
species.description: This Amazonian palm has a single trunk and a crown of pinnate fronds. Its dark fruits develop in hanging clusters.
species.use: Riverside and Indigenous communities eat the fruit and use its oil in food.
species.fireNote: Fallen fronds can add coarse surface fuel after drying.

sources.title: Physicochemical characteristics and lipid profile of bacaba
Plants of the World Online: Oenocarpus bacaba

species.plainUse: People eat the fruit and use its oil in food.

species.name: Broad sword fern
species.description: This fern makes a tuft of long fronds with many narrow pinnae. It can grow on soil or on other plants in humid tropical habitats.
species.use: Records from Asia describe young fronds eaten and ornamental cultivation.
species.fireNote: Dry litter can collect below green fronds.

sources.title: PROSEA: Nephrolepis biserrata
Plants of the World Online: Nephrolepis biserrata

species.plainUse: It is grown as an ornamental plant. We have no local use recorded here.

species.name: Brazil nut tree
species.description: This large Amazonian tree produces heavy woody fruits that contain edible seeds. Mature trees can stand above the surrounding forest canopy.
species.use: Brazil nut harvest is a major non-timber forest product and livelihood activity. Kayapó harvest and dispersal practices have also been linked to seedling recruitment in groves.
species.fireNote: Fire can damage large trees and seedlings.

sources.title: Anthropogenic Landscape in Southeastern Amazonia
The evolving role of Bertholletia excelsa in Amazonia

species.plainUse: Families gather Brazil nuts for food and sale.

species.name: Açaí palm
species.description: This floodplain palm grows as several slender stems from a common base. It produces small dark fruits in branched clusters.
species.use: Families in the Brazilian Amazon harvest and process the fruit as food and a market product.
species.fireNote: Fallen fronds can add surface fuel after drying.

sources.title: Non-Wood Forest Product Extractivism: A Case Study of Euterpe oleracea
Morphoagronomic and molecular characterization of Euterpe oleracea

species.plainUse: Families harvest açaí fruit for food and sale.

species.name: Buriti palm
species.description: This tall palm forms dense stands in wet Amazonian areas. Its large fan leaves rise above a thick trunk.
species.use: People in Amazonian communities use its fruit pulp and oil as food and its leaves and fibers for household materials. Harvest methods can affect palm survival.
species.fireNote: Wetland water can limit fire at some times, but drought can change exposure.

sources.title: Mauritia flexuosa: an Amazonian palm to cultivate in Peru
Managing Amazonian palms for community use

species.plainUse: People use its fruit for food and its leaves and fibres to make household items.

species.name: Para rubber tree
species.description: This tree is native to Amazonia and has compound leaves that are shed seasonally. Its trunk contains latex vessels.
species.use: People tap the latex to make natural rubber. Embrapa records rubber tapping as an Amazon livelihood.
species.fireNote: Shed leaves can add litter after drying.

sources.title: Produção de borracha natural de seringueira: histórico e caminho a seguir
Novas Tecnologias na Produção da Borracha Natural no Amazonas

species.plainUse: People tap its milky sap to make natural rubber.

species.name: Cupuaçu
species.description: This Amazonian relative of cacao has large leaves and heavy brown fruits. The fruit pulp has a strong aroma and pale color.
species.use: Farmers grow it for pulp used in drinks, frozen foods and preserves. Seeds can also be processed into a cacao-like fat and food products.
species.fireNote: Orchard litter can dry between rains.

sources.title: Cupuaçuzeiro: nutrição, calagem e adubação
Cupuaçu in natura

species.plainUse: Farmers grow its fruit for drinks and preserves.

species.name: Cassava
species.description: Cassava is a shrub with palmate leaves and swollen storage roots. Varieties differ in growth form, root chemistry and food preparation.
species.use: Amazonian farmers cultivate cassava as a staple crop. Toxic varieties require processing before eating.
species.fireNote: Crop residues can dry after harvest.

sources.title: Reliance Upon a Toxic Staple Crop: Tukanoan Cultivation of Manioc
Origin and Domestication of Native Amazonian Crops

species.plainUse: Farmers grow cassava for food. Some varieties must be processed to remove toxins.

species.name: Andiroba
species.description: This Amazonian tree has compound leaves and large seeds in woody fruits. It occurs in floodplain forests and other humid forest settings.
species.use: Communities extract seed oil for local medicine, repellents, soap and markets. Timber and seed harvest require management because the tree is a multiple-use resource.
species.fireNote: Leaves, seeds and wood can occupy different fuel layers.

sources.title: Population Structure and Fruit Production of Carapa guianensis
Práticas de uso e manejo tradicional de Carapa spp.

species.plainUse: People collect its seeds for oil used in soap and traditional medicine.

species.name: Copaíba
species.description: This Amazonian tree produces oleoresin in trunk tissues. Its leaves are compound and its crown can be broad.
species.use: Amazonian communities collect copaiba oleoresin for traditional medicine and local trade. Traditional use does not establish medical safety or efficacy.
species.fireNote: Woody litter can add fuel after drying.

sources.title: Brazilian Amazon Traditional Medicine and the Treatment of Difficult to Heal Leishmaniasis Wounds with Copaifera
In vitro and in vivo antimalarial potential of Copaifera reticulata oleoresin

species.plainUse: People collect its resin for trade and traditional medicine. Traditional use does not prove that a remedy is safe or effective.

species.name: Guaraná
species.description: Guaraná is a woody plant with compound leaves and red fruits that expose dark seeds. It is native to the central Amazon and is also cultivated.
species.use: Sateré-Mawé and other Amazonian producers process the seeds into a stimulant food and drink.
species.fireNote: Cultivation residues can dry after harvest.

sources.title: Guaraná: Ecological and social perspectives on an economic plant
Guarana: Revisiting a highly caffeinated plant from the Amazon

species.plainUse: Sateré-Mawé and other Amazonian producers use the seeds in foods and drinks.

species.name: Peach palm
species.description: This palm often has several spiny stems and pinnate leaves. Cultivated forms produce clusters of starchy fruits and can also be managed for palm hearts.
species.use: Indigenous peoples domesticated peach palm for fruit and other products. Farmers still grow landraces for food and palm heart in Amazonian systems.
species.fireNote: Fallen leaf bases can add local fuel.

sources.title: Origin and Dispersal of Domesticated Peach Palm
Domestication of Peach Palm in Southwestern Amazonia

species.plainUse: Farmers grow peach palm for its fruit and palm heart.

species.name: Tucumã-do-Pará
species.description: This eastern Amazon palm has a spiny trunk and pinnate leaves. Its orange fruit pulp surrounds a hard seed.
species.use: People eat the fruit fresh and use fruit, fiber and seed products in local economies.
species.fireNote: Spiny leaf bases and fallen fronds can add local fuel after drying.

Astrocaryum aculeatum e A. vulgare: tucumã-do-amazonas e tucumã-do-pará

species.plainUse: People eat the fruit and use the plant's fibres.

humanEvidence.title: Food and non-timber livelihoods
humanEvidence.summary: Brazil nuts, açaí, buriti, bacaba and tucumã are documented food or non-timber products. Harvest income depends on access, processing, markets and local management.

humanEvidence.title: Cultivation and domestication
humanEvidence.summary: Cassava, guaraná, cupuaçu and peach palm show that Amazonian food systems include selection, planting and processing. A crop record does not identify a crop at the imagined settlement.

humanEvidence.title: Agriculture and fire coordination
humanEvidence.summary: Research in southeastern Amazonia links land use, ignition practices, repeated fire and grass invasion in some landscapes. It does not identify the cause, intensity or species in this training scenario.

humanEvidence.title: Voluntary carbon market and Verra project accounting
humanEvidence.summary: Verra VCUs are issued for verified project reductions or removals. Projects set a baseline, show that the action is additional, monitor results, address leakage and protect against reversal over time. Credits are issued for projects, not for species or photos.

humanEvidence.title: Community and biodiversity safeguards
humanEvidence.summary: Biodiversity and community claims need their own evidence and participation processes. A field catalogue can support learning, but it is not a VCS validation, investment advice or legal opinion.
